title: Evaluate animal anatomy and physiology systems

lessons.title: Body systems and how they work together
lessons.html:
Why anatomy and physiology matter to a production manager

Anatomy is the structure of the animal's body; physiology is how those structures work. A manager who understands both can judge why a Bonsmara cow conceives late, why a feedlot steer bloats or why an Angora goat loses condition in a cold snap. Evaluation means looking at a system, asking whether it is functioning normally, and linking what you see to management, nutrition, genetics or disease.

The main body systems

SystemMain partsProduction link
Skeletal and muscularBones, joints, musclesCarcass yield, mobility, lameness
DigestiveMouth, stomach(s), intestines, liverFeed conversion, growth, milk
RespiratoryNostrils, trachea, lungsHeat tolerance, pneumonia risk
CirculatoryHeart, blood vessels, bloodOxygen and nutrient transport
ReproductiveOvaries, uterus, testesCalving rate, lambing percentage
Nervous and endocrineBrain, nerves, glands, hormonesBehaviour, stress, cycles
Urinary and integumentKidneys, bladder, skin, hair, woolWater balance, fibre and hide quality

Systems are linked

No system works alone. Heat stress in a Holstein cow on a KwaZulu-Natal dairy raises breathing rate (respiratory), shifts blood to the skin (circulatory), lowers feed intake (digestive) and reduces conception (reproductive, through hormone changes). Homeostasis is the body's effort to keep temperature, water, blood sugar and acidity stable. When the demand on the animal is greater than its ability to adapt, production drops first, then health.

When you evaluate a herd, start with simple observations: body condition score, rumination, dung consistency, breathing rate, gait, coat and fertility records. Each clue points to one or more systems. Record what you see so that trends can be compared between camps and seasons.

lessons.title: Digestive systems: ruminants and monogastrics
lessons.html:
Comparing digestive systems

Farm animals fall into two broad groups. Ruminants (cattle, sheep, goats) have a four-compartment stomach: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum. Monogastrics (pigs, poultry) have a simple stomach, much like humans. Horses are hind-gut fermenters: a simple stomach with a large caecum and colon where fibre is fermented.

The rumen

The rumen is a fermentation vat holding billions of bacteria, protozoa and fungi. These microbes break down cellulose in veld grass, hay and crop residues into volatile fatty acids, which the animal absorbs as its main energy source. Microbes also turn non-protein nitrogen, such as urea in a lick, into microbial protein that the animal digests further down. Rumination (chewing the cud) reduces particle size and adds saliva, which buffers rumen acidity.

  • Sudden changes to high-starch diets (maize grain) can cause acidosis because acid builds up faster than saliva can buffer it.
  • Frothy bloat can occur on lush lucerne or clover when gas is trapped in foam.
  • Young calves and lambs bypass the rumen through the oesophageal groove when suckling, so milk goes straight to the abomasum.

Monogastric digestion

Pigs and chickens rely on their own enzymes in the stomach and small intestine. They digest starch, fats and good-quality protein efficiently but use fibre poorly, so their rations are grain and oilcake based and must supply essential amino acids such as lysine directly. Poultry have a crop for storage and a gizzard that grinds food.

Evaluating the digestive system

Watch rumination (a healthy resting cow spends many hours a day chewing the cud), dung consistency, rumen fill on the left flank and feed intake. Loose, bubbly dung or many cows not ruminating after a ration change warns of a digestive upset that needs action and possibly your vet.

lessons.title: Reproduction, respiration and circulation
lessons.html:
Systems that drive reproduction and performance

Reproductive physiology

In the cow, the ovary releases an egg roughly every three weeks under the control of hormones from the brain and ovary. Oestrus (heat) is the short period when she will stand to be mounted. Signs include restlessness, mounting others, clear mucus and a swollen vulva. Ewes and does are seasonal breeders in many regions, cycling mainly as day length shortens in autumn, which is why many SA sheep farmers mate in late summer to autumn.

In the bull or ram, testes produce sperm and testosterone. Scrotal circumference and a breeding soundness examination by a vet are practical ways to evaluate fertility before the mating season. Poor nutrition, heat stress and diseases such as trichomonosis or vibriosis reduce conception, so reproductive records must be read together with feed and health records.

Respiratory and circulatory systems

Lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide; the heart pumps blood carrying oxygen, nutrients, hormones and heat around the body. Normal ranges for temperature, pulse and breathing rate differ between species and with age, activity and weather. Use the reference values in your animal health manual or from your vet, and take readings on calm animals at rest.

  • Fast, laboured breathing with fever can indicate pneumonia, common in feedlot calves after transport.
  • Pale gums or inner eyelids suggest anaemia, for example from wireworm in sheep.
  • Swelling under the jaw (bottle jaw) can accompany severe parasite anaemia.

Putting the evaluation together

Combine observation, records and, where needed, veterinary tests. Ask: which system is under strain, what caused it, and what management change will fix it? Then check whether the change worked.

Key points

  • Body systems are linked; stress in one affects others and production.
  • Ruminants rely on rumen microbes to digest fibre; monogastrics need concentrated, high-quality feed.
  • Sudden diet changes can cause acidosis or bloat.
  • Reproductive success depends on hormones, nutrition, health and heat stress.
  • Use species reference values and your vet when judging temperature, pulse and breathing.
